headline_marked: [[12-year-old launches DOJO FEED]], a social network for devs aged 5-18, adults blocked
headline: 12-year-old launches DOJO FEED, a social network for devs aged 5-18, adults blocked
summary: Built entirely on a POCO C55 phone, this new platform offers a dedicated space for young coders, free from adult influence and the intimidation of mainstream sites.
details: DOJO FEED, a new social network, has been launched by a 12-year-old developer, exclusively for coders aged 5-18. The platform strictly blocks adults, ensuring a safe space for young talent to connect and share their work. It was notably built entirely on a POCO C55 phone.

The creator's motivation stems from the intimidating nature of existing platforms, where young developers' early projects often get lost amidst professional discussions. DOJO FEED aims to provide a 'dojo' where a 'Hello World' receives the same respect as a shipped SaaS.

Features are intentionally minimal: a simple feed, posts with optional code snippets, likes, and the ability to delete one's own content. This streamlined approach focuses on core functionality to ensure a quick and effective launch.

The technical stack includes a single HTML file, Supabase for authentication and database management, and Netlify for hosting. This lean setup allowed the young developer to build and deploy the platform using only a mobile device.

headline_marked: [[US tightens drone & robot restrictions]], but China's scale advantage remains global
headline: US tightens drone & robot restrictions, but China's scale advantage remains global
summary: Washington imposed steep tariffs on foreign-made drones and advanced robotic systems, citing national security. This move aims to restrict foreign tech, but analysts predict a fragmented global market rather than a clean split.
details: In July and August, the U.S. tightened restrictions on foreign-made advanced robotic systems and imposed steep tariffs on imported drones and their components. These moves, citing national-security concerns, are part of a broader effort to restrict foreign technology in strategically important industries.

The FCC’s Covered List, initially targeting telecommunications and surveillance equipment, has expanded to include foreign-made drones and advanced robotic devices. The drone tariffs are set to take effect in September, with additional component tariffs following in 2027.

These restrictions come as Chinese manufacturers have established commanding positions in both drones and humanoid robots, often offering prices that U.S. and European rivals struggle to match. The world's five largest humanoid robot makers by shipments in H1 2026 were all Chinese, accounting for 86% of global shipments.

Industry analysts suggest the restrictions may lead to a fragmented global market rather than a clean U.S.-China split. Chinese companies are expected to expand into other regions, while U.S. and allied manufacturers compete in markets prioritizing security requirements.

China's dominance in manufacturing scale and cost advantages allows its companies to put more robots into use, generating data that improves technology and further drives down costs. Chinese humanoid makers are also integrating more of the technology stack in-house, leveraging an existing manufacturing base.

While the United States leads in frontier AI, software, and semiconductor innovation, China excels in manufacturing scale, supply-chain depth, and cost. This manufacturing edge enables Chinese companies to reduce humanoid prices faster than most U.S. competitors can match.

Chinese robotics companies are already targeting price-sensitive markets with severe labor shortages across Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. Experts anticipate a path similar to Chinese electric-vehicle companies: building scale domestically, expanding overseas, and eventually establishing local production.
